1.title: Your very first Python program.
1.description: Discover what Python is, why millions of developers love it, and write your first working line of code.

sections.title: What is Python?
paragraphs: Python is a general-purpose programming language created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991. Its design philosophy puts readability first — Python code is meant to look almost like plain English, so you spend less time deciphering syntax and more time solving real problems.

Because of that simplicity, Python has become one of the most popular languages on the planet. You will find it everywhere: data scientists use it to analyse millions of rows, web engineers build backends with it, game developers script logic in it, and AI researchers train models with it.
Most importantly for you right now: Python is a fantastic first language. If you can describe an idea in plain words, you are already halfway to writing Python.

takeaway.label: WHY PYTHON?
takeaway.text: Easy to read, powerful enough for professionals, and in demand everywhere from startups to NASA.

sections.title: The print() function
paragraphs: The very first thing most programmers learn is how to make a program say something. In Python, you do that with the built-in print() function.

A function is a reusable action with a name. You call it by writing its name followed by parentheses. Whatever you place inside the parentheses is called an argument — the value you hand to the function so it can do its job.
Wrapping text in quotes (" " or ' ') tells Python you mean a literal piece of text, not a variable or command. That piece of text is called a string.

codeExample.caption: One function call. One string argument. One line of output.

sections.title: print() can do more than greet the world
paragraphs: You are not limited to one message per program. You can call print() as many times as you like — each call prints on its own line.
You can also print numbers directly without quotes. Python knows 42 is a number, not text, so no quotes are needed.

codeExample.code:
print("I am learning Python!")
print("One line at a time.")
print(2025)
codeExample.caption: Three calls, three lines of output — in order, top to bottom.

takeaway.label: THE TAKEAWAY
takeaway.text: Python runs your code line by line, from top to bottom. Each print() call adds one new line to the output.

exercises.title: Sum of even numbers
exercises.description: Given a list of integers numbers, return the sum of all even numbers in the list. An even number is divisible by 2 with no remainder.
exercises.outputDescription: An integer — the sum of all even numbers in the list.

examples.explanation: The even numbers are 2, 4, and 6. Their sum is 12.
There are no even numbers, so the result is 0.

hints.label: A Little Nudge
hints.sublabel: Think about how to check if a number is even.
hints.content: An even number leaves no remainder when divided by 2. In Python, you can check this with the modulo operator: number % 2 == 0. How might you use this check as you go through the list?

hints.label: Guide Me Further
hints.sublabel: Think about which tools to use.
hints.content: Consider using a for loop to iterate over each element in the list. Keep a running total (a variable that starts at 0 and grows). Inside the loop, only add to the total when the number is even. This is a classic accumulator pattern.

hints.label: Show Me the Approach
hints.content:
Here's pseudocode for one clean approach: 
function sum_even(numbers):
    total = 0
    for each number in numbers:
        if number % 2 == 0:
            total = total + number
    return total
You initialise a total variable to 0, loop through every element, and only add it when it passes the even-number check. No external libraries needed — just a loop, a condition, and an accumulator.

exercises.title: Reverse a string
exercises.description: Given a string s, return it reversed.

hints.label: A Little Nudge
hints.content: What if you built the result one character at a time, starting from the end of the string? In Python, you can access individual characters with their index.

hints.label: Guide Me Further
hints.content: Python strings support slicing with a step argument. The notation s[start:stop:step] lets you control direction. What step value would read a string backwards?

hints.label: Show Me the Approach
hints.content:
Python's slice notation makes this a one-liner: 
def reverse_string(s):
    return s[::-1]
s[::-1] starts at the end, moves to the beginning, one character at a time — returning the reversed string.

exercises.title: Count vowels
exercises.description: Given a string s, return the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) in the string. Treat uppercase and lowercase letters the same.

examples.explanation: The vowels are e, o, o.

hints.label: A Little Nudge
hints.content: You need to check each character in the string. How can you tell if a character is a vowel? Consider keeping a list (or string) of all vowels and checking if the character is in it.

hints.label: Guide Me Further
hints.content: Convert the whole string (or each character) to lowercase before checking. That way "A" and "a" are treated the same. The in operator checks membership: "a" in "aeiou" returns True.

hints.label: Show Me the Approach
hints.content:
def count_vowels(s):
    count = 0
    for char in s.lower():
        if char in "aeiou":
            count += 1
    return count
You can also do this in one line with a generator expression: sum(1 for c in s.lower() if c in "aeiou").

exercises.title: Find maximum
exercises.description: Given a non-empty list of integers numbers, return the largest number in the list without using the built-in max() function.

hints.label: A Little Nudge
hints.sublabel: Think about how you'd do this by hand.
hints.content: If you were scanning a list of numbers by hand, you'd probably keep track of the biggest one you've seen so far. How could you replicate that in code?

hints.label: Guide Me Further
hints.content: Start with current_max set to the first element. Then loop through the rest. If you find something bigger, update current_max. What should happen at the end of the loop?

hints.label: Show Me the Approach
hints.content:
def find_maximum(numbers):
    current_max = numbers[0]
    for num in numbers[1:]:
        if num > current_max:
            current_max = num
    return current_max
Starting with the first element avoids issues with negative numbers (unlike starting with 0).
